record.paper_title: Open Problems on Open Algebraic Varieties (Montreal 1994 Problems)
record.original_question: Suppose p is a polynomial in two variables over C whose zero set is smooth, irreducible, and rational. Must p be a factor of a field generator, equivalently of a generically rational polynomial? In other words, does there always exist a polynomial q such that the generic fiber of pq is rational?

evidence.quote:
QUESTION 3. If the polynomial p in two variables over C has smooth, irreducible
rational zero set, is p a factor of a field generator (or generically rational polynomial), i.e.
does there exist a polynomial q such that the generic fibre of pq is rational ?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Work over the field of complex numbers C. A polynomial f ∈ C[x,y] is called a field generator if there exists a polynomial g ∈ C[x,y] such that C(f, g) = C(x, y); equivalently, f is a field generator if and only if its generic fibre is a rational curve (such an f is also called a generically rational polynomial). Say that p ∈ C[x,y] is a factor of a field generator if there exists q ∈ C[x,y] such that pq is a field generator, i.e. such that the generic fibre of pq is rational.

Suppose p ∈ C[x,y] is a polynomial whose zero set V(p) ⊂ C^2 is smooth, irreducible, and a rational curve. Must p be a factor of a field generator? Equivalently, does there always exist q ∈ C[x,y] such that the generic fibre of pq is a rational curve?
artifact.status_search_result: Web searches for the status of this question (factorization of polynomials in C[x,y] with smooth rational zero set as factors of generically rational polynomials / field generators, in the spirit of the Montreal 1994 open problems on open algebraic varieties) did not return a clear resolution. No subsequent paper announcing a proof or counterexample was located, so the current status could not be verified.
